faqs_subtitle: Everything you need to know about disaster recovery with KubeDB

faqs.question: What RPO and RTO can I expect?
faqs.answer: With automatic failover, recovery typically takes about a minute by default. With asynchronous replication, data loss is a few seconds at most, and with synchronous replication it is zero. Planned switchovers are always zero data loss. Your actual numbers depend on your network and workload, so measure them in a drill.

faqs.question: Which failover style should I choose?
faqs.answer: Choose automatic failover when a data center failover must not wait for a person, you run many databases, and you can host a small third site to break ties. Choose manual failover when your team must approve every move, you have only two sites, or you want the smallest footprint. Choose active-active distributed SQL for new services that need zero loss and near-zero downtime and can accept the application changes.

faqs.question: What does synchronous replication cost?
faqs.answer: Each write waits for the standby, so write latency grows by one network round trip between the data centers. In exchange, a lost data center loses no committed data. Many teams turn it on only for the databases that need it.

faqs.question: When should I use active-active?
faqs.answer: When you need zero data loss and near-zero downtime and can keep your data centers close together. A distributed SQL database keeps a full copy in each data center. It requires application changes, so it suits new services best.

faqs.question: Is there always only one writable primary?
faqs.answer: In standard active/standby setups, yes. KubeDB keeps one data center in charge at a time, and the other follows. Active-active distributed SQL is the exception, by design.

faqs.question: Which databases does this cover?
faqs.answer: KubeDB protects many of the popular relational, NoSQL, streaming, and search engines across data centers, using the best mechanism for each one. For some engines replication is asynchronous, so data loss equals the replication delay. See the documentation for the full list.

faqs.question: How do you prevent two sites from acting as primary?
faqs.answer: KubeDB makes sure only one data center is in charge at any moment, even during a network split. A site that loses contact stops accepting writes until it is safe to continue.

faqs.question: What happens when the failed data center comes back?
faqs.answer: It rejoins as a standby and KubeDB brings it back in sync. When you are ready, a planned switchover returns the primary role with no data lost.

faqs.question: Does this include backup and point-in-time recovery?
faqs.answer: Yes. KubeDB provides encrypted, incremental backups with point-in-time recovery, so you can recover from failures that replication would copy to the standby, such as an accidental delete.

faqs.question: How do I know my targets are met?
faqs.answer: Run planned switchovers and scheduled disaster recovery drills, for example quarterly, and record the RPO and RTO each drill measures. KubeDB shows status and progress at every step.

faqs.question: Is this running in production?
faqs.answer: Yes. KubeDB runs a highly available primary cluster with a live disaster recovery replica at a geographically separate site for a regulated mobile financial services platform. Read the TeleCash case study for details.
